ca-200.Title: Over 200 VR Systems in California Libraries
ca-200.Description: XRLibraries began in 2016 by installing more than 200 virtual reality systems in California public libraries. Its website calls this the largest VR installation in public libraries.

mission.Title: XR Made Easy for Everyone
mission.Description: XRLibraries works with schools and libraries to bring virtual, augmented and mixed reality into their programs and classes. Its stated goal is equitable access to immersive technology for all communities.
mission.Quote: We make XR easy to use for everyone.

headset.Title: A Library VR Headset
headset.Description: Standalone headsets let a library visitor stand on the moon, swim a coral reef or practice a job, with no computer attached. Meta Quest and Pico both appear on XRLibraries’ partner list, and its Nevada headsets run on Pico.
headset.Partners: Meta Quest and Pico are listed partners

nv-2017.Title: Nevada Follows Marin County
nv-2017.Description: In 2017 Nevada’s state library put its first VR headsets in public libraries: 22 headsets in 11 libraries, with STEM content. WorkingNation reports that the model followed a program at the Marin County Free Library in California.

cil-talks.Title: XR at Computers in Libraries
cil-talks.Description: XRLibraries’ executive director, John MacLeod, presented “Integrating XR Tech & Programming in Libraries” at Computers in Libraries Connect in 2020 and “Using XR to Discover ‘Lost Stories’ & Pop-Up Books” in 2022.

sandi.Title: Project SANDI
sandi.Description: Supporting and Advancing Nevada’s Dislocated Individuals began during the 2020 downturn with a $13.8 million federal grant. It uses VR to explore careers in five fields: skilled trades, healthcare, IT, advanced manufacturing and logistics.
sandi.More: The program grew to more than 1,000 headsets at over 80 locations, with 35 VR field trips and five training simulations, including dialysis technician and certified nursing assistant. XRLibraries’ executive director is a partner in the project.
sandi.Partners: Nevada Governor’s Office of Economic Development, XRLibraries

nv-1100.Title: 1,100 Headsets in Nevada
nv-1100.Description: XRLibraries and Lifeliqe installed VR headsets in Nevada’s community college and public libraries. XRLibraries’ homepage counts more than 1,100.
nv-1100.More: XRLibraries uses ArborXR to set up headsets and send updates remotely. Its director told ArborXR the switch cut the time and resources spent by about 60 percent.
nv-1100.Where: Nevada community college and public libraries

dialysis.Title: Training From a Town of 300
dialysis.Description: A remote 12-week dialysis technician certification lets people train without traveling to a training center. In a community of about 300 people, a single mother finished the program, passed her certification and plans to become a registered nurse.
dialysis.Quote: It brought the dialysis concepts to life.
dialysis.QuoteBy: Natasha York, former library assistant, in WorkingNation

playbooks.Title: XR Playbooks
playbooks.Description: XRLibraries catalogs more than 300 XR apps in categories from astronomy and history to mindfulness and music, then bundles them into themed playbooks that come pre-installed on library headsets.

showcase.Title: XR Showcase
showcase.Description: In this video series, hosts George and Camila try VR and AR apps for libraries, from Tilt Brush and Wander to Apollo 11 VR, and share practical tips like cleaning headsets and setting a guardian boundary.
showcase.More: Episodes also cover running big VR events with rotating stations, recording video inside a headset and playing media through the Meta Quest TV app.

way-out.Title: A Way Out of No Way
way-out.Description: Marin City students who call themselves the Marinovators built a VR experience of the World War II shipyards and life in Marin City, plus a musical tribute to the African-American workers whose stories were rarely told.
way-out.More: The project ran in three tracks: immersive storytelling, music and VR modeling. It is part of XRLibraries’ Lost Stories work, which plans to look for Latino, Asian-Pacific and Native American stories next.

charleston.Title: The Black Wall Street of Charleston
charleston.Description: Career and technical education students at Burke High School built an augmented-reality scavenger hunt that leads players to Charleston’s Black-owned businesses.
charleston.Partners: Burke High School CTE students, Preservation Society of Charleston, Burke High School Foundation

seeking.Title: Seeking Immortality
seeking.Description: A browser-based VR world, funded by an IMLS Native American Enhancement Grant, that preserves endangered Cheyenne language and cultural knowledge. Tribal members and students learned 3D scanning so the tribe keeps control of its own data.
seeking.Partners: Northern Cheyenne Tribe, SJSU School of Information

ukraine.Title: Children Draw War, Not Flowers
ukraine.Description: An immersive 3D exhibition of art by children in Ukraine’s Cherkasy region, which took in more than 42,000 displaced children. It helps children work through war-related trauma, preserves their artwork, and was honored at the Anthem Awards.
ukraine.Partners: SJSU School of Information, Ukrainian librarians, children and veterans, 40 regional libraries

pollinators.Title: Pollinators at the Marin County Fair
pollinators.Description: At XRLibraries’ bug-themed booth, fairgoers used an AR app called Pollinators to plant flowers and release monarch butterflies that flew around pollinating them. Marin artist Cynthia Jensen lent bug sculptures for the booth.

freedom.Title: Freedom to Read
freedom.Description: A VR environment that helps citizens, librarians and students fight book bans, and helps young people in affected areas find challenged books that reflect their lives. It is one of the shared worlds listed on XRLibraries’ metaverse page.
freedom.Partners: SJSU School of Information, Unite Against Book Bans, Little Free Library, Books Unbanned

lib-globe.Title: The Globe
lib-globe.Description: A terrestrial globe on a brass stand. Every library kept one long before anyone could look a place up in a second: it is the original way to see where a story is set. The places in the books on these shelves are all on it somewhere.

lib-desk.Title: The Reference Desk
lib-desk.Description: Where you ask. Librarians were the first search engine: this is the desk where a question gets answered, a book gets found and a visitor gets pointed the right way. Nobody has ever been turned away from one for not knowing what they were looking for.
lib-desk.Where: The Reading Room, by the hall

lib-table-north.Title: The North Reading Table
lib-table-north.Description: A long oak table under three green-shaded banker's lamps. The lamps throw their light down on to the page and keep it out of your eyes, which is why reading rooms have used them for over a century. Sit anywhere: the chairs are leather and the table is meant to be leaned on.

lib-table-south.Title: The South Reading Table
lib-table-south.Description: The second of the room's two reading tables, a mirror of the first across the hall. Rooms like this were built so that anyone could walk in off the street and sit down with a book for nothing, which is the oldest promise a public library makes.

lib-piano.Title: The Grand Piano
lib-piano.Description: A grand piano with its lid propped open, turned so the keyboard faces the room. Libraries have always been about more than books: lectures, readings, recitals. The lid is up because a grand is meant to be heard across a room this size, and the bench is out because someone was just playing.

lib-stair.Title: The Spiral Stair
lib-stair.Description: Nineteen treads winding round a brass newel, up to the gallery that runs right round the room. The upper shelves are up there. Go on up: the handrail climbs with you, and the gallery is wide enough to walk the whole way round and look down on the hall.

lib-window.Title: The Arched Window
lib-window.Description: The room's one great window, set in the west wall so the afternoon sun comes straight down the hall. Reading rooms were laid out this way before electric light: the tables sit where the daylight falls. Beyond the glass are the hills.

lib-gallery.Title: The Gallery
lib-gallery.Description: You made it up. The gallery runs round all four walls behind a panelled parapet, with the upper shelves at your shoulder and the whole hall laid out below: the checkered floor, the runner, the chandeliers at eye level. The quietest seat in the building is the one you are standing in.
lib-gallery.Where: The Reading Room, up the spiral stair

wax-2016.Title: The First Headsets
wax-2016.Description: In 2016, libraries in Marin County, California, began offering virtual reality stations as the pilot for the California Virtual Reality Experience. XRLibraries launched that year as the project’s coordinator. Teen volunteers helped first-time visitors into headsets and guided them through their first worlds.
wax-2016.More: Library Journal reported that four Marin County libraries had offered VR stations since 2016, with teens from the Marin WebStars volunteer program helping manage the stations and guide new users.
wax-2016.Partners: Califa, Marin County Free Library, XRLibraries

wax-2017a.Title: VR Goes Statewide
wax-2017a.Description: In June 2017 the California State Library, Oculus and the library consortium Califa partnered to bring VR-ready PCs with Rift headsets to more than 90 libraries across California, building on the Marin County pilot. XRLibraries, launched in 2016 as the project’s coordinator, also became a clearinghouse where libraries share what works with VR and AR.
wax-2017a.More: XRLibraries’ website counts more than 200 VR systems installed in California public libraries, and calls it the largest VR installation in public libraries.

wax-2017b.Title: Story Time in 3D
wax-2017b.Description: Library Journal reported in 2017 that young children loved virtual reality story times, while teens gravitated to VR games. In Marin, children listened to stories inside three-dimensional worlds.
wax-2017b.Partners: Libraries in the California Virtual Reality Experience

wax-2018a.Title: Nevada Opens Its Stations
wax-2018a.Description: Nevada’s state library set aside $22,000 of a 2017 budget increase for a VR pilot: 22 headsets loaded with STEM content in 11 libraries, modeled on Marin County’s program. In February 2018 the Carson City Library’s grand re-opening featured VR and AR stations, and XRLibraries’ founder presented in a webinar for librarians across the state.
wax-2018a.Where: Carson City Library and other Nevada libraries

wax-2019a.Title: VR on the Road
wax-2019a.Description: Marin’s VR program went out into the community: to schools, senior centers, the county fair, and people displaced by deadly wildfires.

wax-2019b.Title: VR in the World’s Catalog
wax-2019b.Description: Nevada’s state library and its partner XRLibraries set out to catalog VR content so any library could find it. In 2019 Nevada librarians led a first-of-its-kind effort to catalog virtual reality in WorldCat, the world’s largest library catalog, and planned a cataloging hack-a-thon in Marin, California and Carson City, Nevada.
wax-2019b.More: Nevada’s Governor’s Office of Economic Development says a Carson City librarian cataloged the first VR course companion in WorldCat, and that the work produced a collection of more than 1,000 3D interactive VR objects.

wax-2019c.Title: XR Marin and the XR Stars
wax-2019c.Description: XR Marin brought together the Marin County Free Library, XRLibraries, Novato Unified School District and the Marin County Office of Education. Teens served as “XR Stars,” helping patrons use the equipment. Its programs let people make 3D models, design 3D games and produce 360-degree video tours, and one teen at a VR summer camp borrowed the cameras and filmed her family’s farm.
wax-2019c.Partners: Marin County Free Library, XRLibraries, Novato Unified School District, Marin County Office of Education

wax-2020.Title: Project SANDI
wax-2020.Description: In October 2020 Nevada won a $13.8 million federal grant for Project SANDI (Supporting and Advancing Nevada’s Dislocated Individuals), which uses VR to explore careers in skilled trades, healthcare, IT, advanced manufacturing and logistics. It grew to more than 1,000 headsets at over 80 locations. XRLibraries’ executive director is a partner in the project.
wax-2020.Partners: Nevada Governor’s Office of Workforce Innovation, Governor’s Office of Economic Development, Nevada libraries and colleges

wax-2022a.Title: 360° Stories in Washington
wax-2022a.Description: XRLibraries was the trainer for the Washington State Library’s VR 360 grant program. In 2022 it helped six libraries create 360-degree virtual reality stories about topics important to their communities. The program was open to public, tribal and academic libraries and funded by IMLS through the Library Services and Technology Act.

wax-2022b.Title: Lost Stories
wax-2022b.Description: In Marin City, students who call themselves the Marinovators built a VR experience of the World War II shipyards and life in Marin City, plus a musical tribute to the African-American workers whose stories were rarely told. XRLibraries’ director presented its Lost Stories work at Computers in Libraries in 2022.
wax-2022b.More: The project ran in three tracks: immersive storytelling, music and VR modeling.

wax-2024.Title: Children Draw War, Not Flowers
wax-2024.Description: XRLibraries helped design “Children Draw War, Not Flowers,” a browser-based VR art exhibition from the San José State University School of Information. It shows art by Ukrainian children aged 4 to 16 and virtual galleries showing the destruction of Ukrainian libraries, and anyone can visit it free in a web browser.
wax-2024.More: XRLibraries lists the exhibition, which was honored at the Anthem Awards, among its shared worlds.
wax-2024.Partners: SJSU School of Information, Ukrainian librarians and children

wax-2025.Title: Pollinators at the Fair
wax-2025.Description: At the 2025 Marin County Fair, XRLibraries’ bug-themed booth featured Pollinators, an augmented-reality app where fairgoers planted flowers and released monarch butterflies that flew around pollinating them. Marin artist Cynthia Jensen lent bug sculptures for the booth.

Blocks.Text: Extended reality, or XR, is the umbrella word for technology that blends computer-made worlds with the one around you. It covers virtual reality, augmented reality and mixed reality.
Each one changes how much of the real world you still see. Picture a dial that runs from the room you are standing in all the way to a completely made-up place.
Virtual reality, or VR, replaces everything you see with a computer-made world. A headset shows a slightly different picture to each eye, which tricks your brain into seeing depth.

Modern standalone headsets track your head and hands, so you can lean, crouch and reach inside a small play space. One of the first head-mounted displays, built by Ivan Sutherland in 1968, was so heavy it hung from the ceiling.
Augmented reality, or AR, adds digital things to your view of the real world, usually through a phone camera. Seeing a dinosaur in your living room through your phone is AR.

Mixed reality goes a step further: digital objects understand the room, so a virtual ball can bounce off your real table. Many headsets now use passthrough cameras to show your room with digital objects added.

A 360 video is filmed in every direction at once by a camera with two or more lenses. Viewers can look anywhere, but they cannot walk around inside the scene, because the camera recorded from one spot.
That makes 360 video a great way to visit a historic site, a cultural event or a workplace from a library chair, and it is much easier to make than a full 3D world.
A good headset costs hundreds of dollars, and many people have never tried one. Libraries can give everyone a turn, with help from staff who know the equipment.
XR in libraries is not just games. People use it to explore careers, travel to places they cannot reach, save local stories and learn to make immersive media of their own.

ar-around-town.Title: AR Around Town
ar-around-town.Subtitle: Scavenger hunts, fairs and pop-up books

Pages.Heading: Digital layers on the real world

Blocks.Text: Augmented reality adds pictures, sounds and information to the real world, usually through a phone camera. Unlike VR, you stay connected to the place around you.

That makes AR great for walking tours, scavenger hunts, outdoor events and books that pop off the page. XRLibraries’ XR Showcase features LP Bookspace, AR books with friendly characters that explain the story and quiz readers.

Pages.Heading: The Black Wall Street of Charleston

Blocks.Text: Career and technical education students at Burke High School in Charleston, South Carolina, built an AR scavenger hunt featuring Charleston’s Black-owned businesses.
Partners included the Preservation Society of Charleston and the Burke High School Foundation. The hunt works as a history lesson and as a way to support local businesses.
At the 2025 Marin County Fair, XRLibraries’ bug-themed booth featured Pollinators, an AR app where fairgoers planted flowers and released monarch butterflies that flew around pollinating them.
Videos about butterfly migration and pollination, and bug sculptures by Marin artist Cynthia Jensen, rounded out the booth.
Choose five to eight stops that tell one story. Research each stop, then write a short clue and a fun fact for each one.
Ask business owners and property managers for permission, and pick a route with safe sidewalks and crossings.
Walk the route at different times of day. GPS can drift near tall buildings, and screens can be hard to read in bright sun.
Remind players to look up from their phones while they walk. The best AR adds to the real world without making people forget it is there.
A VR program works best when it has a purpose: exploring careers, visiting the ocean floor, learning history or making art. Pick a theme, then choose a few apps that fit it.
XRLibraries groups apps into themed playbooks so a librarian can run a program on day one. Its catalog covers categories like astronomy, history, life science, travel, mindfulness and music.
Charge every headset and test each app. Clear a play area of tables, cords and walls, and set the guardian boundary, the virtual fence that warns players before they bump into something.
Plan how others will watch. Casting the headset view to a TV lets a group follow along, and it keeps the person in the headset from feeling alone.
Headsets touch faces, so clean them between users. XRLibraries’ XR Showcase episodes show how to sanitize headsets and use UV cleaning devices, which matters in any public setting.
Face covers and wipes at every station make cleaning part of the routine instead of an afterthought.
Many visitors have never worn a headset. Start them with something calm and seated, show them how to adjust the fit, and stay close as a spotter.
Keep first sessions short. If someone feels dizzy or uncomfortable, they should take the headset off and rest. Check the headset maker’s age guidance for younger visitors.
At a busy event, set up several stations and rotate headsets between visitors, a tip from the XR Showcase. A sign-up sheet and a timer keep the line moving fairly.
Afterward, ask people what they tried and what they want next. Their answers help you pick the next playbook.

xr-careers.Title: XR for Careers
xr-careers.Subtitle: Try a job before you train for it

Blocks.Text: Virtual reality lets people try a job before they commit to training: stand on a factory floor, look inside a dialysis machine or practice a nursing skill.
In Nevada, a program called Project SANDI put that experience in libraries and community colleges across the state.
SANDI stands for Supporting and Advancing Nevada’s Dislocated Individuals. It began in 2020, during the economic downturn, with a $13.8 million federal grant.
The program focuses on five fields: skilled trades, healthcare, information technology, advanced manufacturing and logistics. It grew to more than 1,000 headsets at over 80 locations.

Pages.Heading: What people do in the headset

Blocks.Text: Visitors take VR field trips to job sites and practice in training simulations for jobs such as dialysis technician, certified nursing assistant and HVAC technician.

A nursing program coordinator at Great Basin College said the headsets allow “personal viewing and repetition of anatomy and pathophysiology.” That kind of repetition is hard to get with real equipment.
Libraries are free, open to everyone and close to home, even in small towns. That makes them a natural place for career exploration.
XRLibraries and its partner Lifeliqe installed VR headsets in Nevada community college and public libraries. XRLibraries’ homepage counts more than 1,100.

Pages.Heading: A story from a small town

Blocks.Text: A remote 12-week dialysis technician certification let people train without traveling to a training center. In a community of about 300 people, a single mother finished the program and passed her certification.
She plans to become a registered nurse. For many rural learners, the library is the closest classroom.

first-job.Title: Your First Job
first-job.Subtitle: Finding it, getting it, keeping it

Blocks.Text: First jobs are often in restaurants, stores, summer camps and farms, or helping neighbors with yard work and babysitting. Think about what you like to do and what you are good at.
Ask family, teachers, coaches and neighbors. Many jobs are found through people you know. In many states, workers under 18 need a work permit, often issued through their school.

A résumé is a one-page summary of you as a worker. Include your contact information, your school, any jobs or volunteer work, skills like languages, computers or tools, and activities that show responsibility.
Keep it neat, short and honest, and ask someone to proofread it.
Before an interview, learn about the business. Dress a little nicer than the job requires and arrive five to ten minutes early.
Give specific examples. “I walked my neighbor’s dogs every day for a summer” shows reliability better than “I’m responsible.” At the end, ask a question about the job and thank the interviewer.
Show up on time, put your phone away and ask questions when you are not sure. Mistakes happen to everyone. Own them and fix them.
Reliability is the quality employers value most in a new worker, and it is how you earn a good reference for your next job.
You must be paid at least the minimum wage, which in many places is higher than the federal minimum. Teens have limits on how many hours they can work on school days.
You have the right to a safe workplace and to speak up about unsafe conditions. If something feels wrong, talk to a trusted adult or your state’s labor office.

making-360.Title: Making 360 Stories
making-360.Subtitle: Film a place so others can stand in it

Blocks.Text: A 360 story is a short video or photo tour filmed in every direction, so viewers can look around as if they were there. It can show a historic site, a cultural event or how something is made from start to finish.

In 2022 the Washington State Library ran a grant program that gave six libraries the equipment and training to make 360 stories about topics important to their communities. XRLibraries was the trainer.
Pick a story that matters locally, and partner with the people who know it best, such as a historical society, a cultural group, a tribe or a local business.
Write a simple shot list: the places to film, who will speak, and what you want viewers to notice in each scene.
Put the camera on a tripod at about eye level, around five feet high, and keep it still. A moving 360 camera can make viewers feel sick.
The camera sees everything, so either step out of the scene or become part of it. Keep important things away from the seam between the lenses, and film in even light.
Sound tells viewers where to look. Record clear narration or interviews, and capture the natural sounds of the place.
Keep each scene short, often 30 to 90 seconds, and give viewers time to look around before the next scene starts.
Stitch the footage in the camera’s app, then share it on headsets, as a 360 video online or in a virtual tour builder. The XR Showcase features Uptale, a platform for building 360 virtual tours.
Save the original files, notes and permissions with your library’s collection so the story lasts.

oral-history.Title: Recording an Oral History
oral-history.Subtitle: How to save the stories of your elders

Blocks.Text: An oral history is a recorded interview with someone about their own memories and experiences. It captures things no newspaper wrote down: how a place smelled, what people joked about, how it felt to live through a flood or a war.
Many of the voices in Lost Stories projects, and in any library’s local history collection, start with interviews like these.
Choose someone whose story you want to save, like a grandparent, a neighbor or an elder. Ask permission, explain why you are recording, and tell them where the recording will be kept.
In many communities, including many Native nations, some stories belong to a family or to the community, so ask who has the right to share them.
Start easy: “Where did you grow up?” Ask open questions that cannot be answered with yes or no, like “What was a normal school day like?” or “Tell me about your first job.”
Ask for details: “What did it look like? Who was there?” Then listen. Silence is fine. People often remember more if you wait.
A phone works well. Find a quiet room away from fans, TVs and kitchens. Set the phone close to the speaker on something soft, and test a short clip first.
At the start, say the date, the place and both of your names. Keep interviews to about an hour so no one gets too tired.
Thank the person and give them a copy. Label the file with names, the date and the place, write a short summary, and keep a backup.
Ask your local library, historical society or tribal archive whether they collect oral histories. Your recording could help someone a hundred years from now.

lost-stories.Title: Lost Stories
lost-stories.Subtitle: Using XR to bring hidden history back

Blocks.Text: History books leave people out. The stories of workers, immigrants, women and communities of color often survive only in family memories, letters and photographs.
XRLibraries calls its work to recover these histories Lost Stories, using XR to bring marginalized history back into view.

Pages.Heading: A Way Out of No Way

Blocks.Text: During World War II, thousands of people came to Marin County to build ships, and many African-American workers and their families lived in Marin City.
Marin City students who call themselves the Marinovators built a VR experience of the shipyard and life in Marin City, with a musical tribute to the Black workers whose stories were rarely told.

Pages.Heading: From a school bus to the Supreme Court

Blocks.Text: Another Lost Stories piece is an animated VR telling of Briggs v. Elliott in South Carolina, a case that grew out of Black families’ fight for a school bus for their children.
Briggs v. Elliott became one of the cases decided together in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954, when the Supreme Court ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional.
XRLibraries plans to search for Latino, Asian-Pacific and Native American lost stories.
Any community can start. Collect oral histories, scan family photos and documents, and ask elders what the official history left out.
Lost stories belong to the people who lived them. Ask permission, credit storytellers if they want credit, and let the community decide how its story is told.
For tribal communities, that can mean keeping some knowledge private. Good projects plan for what should not be shared as carefully as for what should.
A primary source is something made at the time you are studying, by people who were there: a newspaper, a photograph, a letter, a map, a diary or a recorded interview.

A secondary source is made later by someone looking back, like a textbook or a documentary. Primary sources let you meet the past up close. Secondary sources help you see the bigger story around them.

Items: Who made this?
When and where was it made?
Why was it made, and who was it for?
What does it show or say?
What does it leave out?

Blocks.Text: These questions are not about deciding a source is good or bad. They help you understand what each source can and cannot tell you.
Slow down and describe before you decide. In a photograph, look at clothing, signs, tools and the weather. In a newspaper, read the ads as well as the headlines.
Notice the words people used. Some words from the past are now known to be hurtful. Historians study them carefully without repeating them casually.
One source is a clue. Several sources together start to make a case. If a newspaper says a crowd met the first train, does a photograph or a diary agree?
When sources disagree, ask why. Each person saw the event from a different place, with different reasons for remembering it.
Many libraries keep local newspapers, photographs and maps. The Library of Congress runs a free website called Chronicling America with millions of digitized newspaper pages.
Your family is an archive too. Old photos, letters, recipes and the stories your elders tell are primary sources for the history of your town.

Most people will never dive a coral reef, but a headset can take them there. Hydrous, a partner listed by XRLibraries, makes VR experiences of the coral reefs of Palau, with turtles, manta rays and sharks.
Its experiences come with lesson plans and activities, so a visit can turn into a science class.
Corals get much of their food and their color from tiny algae living in their tissues. When the water stays too warm for too long, corals push the algae out and turn white. This is coral bleaching.
Bleached corals are not dead yet, but they are starving. If the water cools in time, the algae can return.
The ocean absorbs a large share of the carbon dioxide people release into the air, roughly a quarter of it. That carbon dioxide makes seawater more acidic.

More acidic water makes it harder for corals, clams, oysters and some plankton to build shells and skeletons. The Stanford Ocean Experience, one of XRLibraries’ environment projects, is a VR experience about this problem.
XRLibraries’ Climate Change Playbook gathers VR apps about climate change for viewing and discussion. The discussion is the important part.
After a VR visit, ask: What surprised you? What would you want to see again? What could our town do?

Pages.Heading: From the ocean to your sink

Blocks.Text: The water in the ocean is connected to the water in your sink through the water cycle. What happens to rivers and rain eventually reaches the sea.
The Water Cycle, on the same shelf, follows a drop of water around the planet.
The water you drink today may once have been part of an ocean, a cloud or a glacier. Earth’s water moves in a loop called the water cycle, powered by energy from the sun.
About 97 percent of Earth’s water is salty ocean water. Less than 3 percent is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers.
Heat from the sun turns liquid water into an invisible gas called water vapor. This is evaporation.
Plants add water vapor too. They pull water up from the soil and release it through tiny pores in their leaves, a process called transpiration.
As moist air rises, it cools. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor, so the vapor condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds.
You can see condensation when a cold glass “sweats” on a hot day.
When cloud droplets join into drops heavy enough to fall, we get precipitation: rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Water collects in oceans, lakes and rivers, soaks into the ground to become groundwater, or is stored as snow and ice. Then the cycle starts again.
In California, much of the year’s water falls as winter snow in the Sierra Nevada. The snowpack works like a frozen reservoir, melting slowly through spring and summer.
In dry years there is less snowpack, and in very wet years rivers can flood. Droughts and floods are part of the same cycle.
Some virtual worlds need a headset or a gaming computer. Others run in a web browser, so anyone with a phone, laptop or library computer can visit.
XRLibraries builds several shared worlds on FrameVR, a browser-based platform it describes as accessible across all devices.
Freedom to Read is a VR environment built with the SJSU School of Information, Unite Against Book Bans, Little Free Library and Books Unbanned.
It helps citizens, librarians and students fight book bans, and helps young people in affected areas find challenged books that reflect their lives.
This immersive 3D exhibition shares art by children in Ukraine’s Cherkasy region, which took in more than 42,000 displaced children after the Russian invasion.

Librarians from 40 regional libraries, veterans and SJSU iSchool faculty and students took part. Funds bought a scanner so libraries could digitize the children’s artwork, and the project was honored at the Anthem Awards.
Built with the Northern Cheyenne Tribe and funded by an IMLS Native American Enhancement Grant, this browser-based world preserves endangered Cheyenne language and cultural knowledge.
Tribal members and students were trained in 3D scanning and other tools to build and manage the space, so the tribe keeps control of its own data.
Start with who it is for and what it should do. Decide what belongs in public, what should stay private, and who gets to make that call.
Make it simple to enter, label everything clearly and test it on a phone. A world only works if people can find their way around.
A computer does not think the way you do. It follows instructions very fast and exactly as written.
A list of step-by-step instructions that solves a problem is called an algorithm. A recipe is an algorithm for cooking. A program is an algorithm written in a language a computer can run.
Inside, computers store everything as bits, which are 1s and 0s. Eight bits make a byte, which can stand for a number from 0 to 255, a letter, or part of a color or a sound.
The letter A, for example, is stored as the number 65, which in binary is 01000001.

Items: Variables are named boxes that hold values, like score = 0.
Conditionals make choices: if the score is more than 10, show “You win!”
Loops repeat steps: for each student in the class, print their name.
Functions bundle steps into a named action you can reuse.

Blocks.Text: Almost every program, from a calculator to a VR game, is built from these few ideas.

total = 0
for each number from 1 to 5:
    total = total + number
show total
This program adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 and shows 15. Change the 5 to 100 and the computer adds the numbers from 1 to 100 just as easily. The answer is 5,050.

A mistake in a program is called a bug. In 1947, engineers working on the Harvard Mark II computer found a real moth stuck in a relay and taped it into their logbook as the “first actual case of bug being found.”
Every programmer writes bugs. Good programmers test their code, read error messages carefully and fix one thing at a time.
Artificial intelligence, or AI, is software that learns patterns from examples instead of following only hand-written rules.
A spam filter learns from millions of emails which ones are junk. A photo app learns what faces look like. A chat assistant learns patterns of language from huge amounts of text.
A language model writes a little bit of text at a time, choosing what is likely to come next based on the patterns it learned. That is why it can write smooth sentences on almost any topic.
It is also why it can state something false in a confident voice. People call these mistakes hallucinations.
Treat AI like a helpful but imperfect study partner. Ask it to explain ideas in different ways, quiz you or give feedback on your writing.
Check important facts against trusted sources. If you use AI for schoolwork, follow your teacher’s rules and be honest about how you used it.
Do not share private information like your address, passwords or photos of other people with AI tools or websites you do not trust.
Images, videos and voices can be made by AI, so a shocking clip online may not be real. Look for the original source before you believe it or share it.
Margaret, Rosa, Mr. Hale and Coach Rae are virtual staff. They answer common questions from what they know about this campus, and when AI is available they can answer more.
They are not real people. A real library would decide what its own guides know and how they speak.

world-builder.Title: World Builder’s Handbook
world-builder.Subtitle: How to make 3D worlds and games like this campus

Blocks.Text: Before any 3D work, decide who your world is for and what they will do there. Write one sentence: “In this world, you can …”

This campus began as a list: a museum that tells a story, a library you can read in, a school where every class is hands-on and a recess yard for fun. Then came a rough map on paper showing how to walk from one to the next.
Start small. A single room that works beats a giant world that doesn’t.
You can build real 3D worlds with free tools:

Items: three.js: draws 3D in a web page. This campus runs on it.
Blender: free, professional software for modeling, sculpting and animation.
Godot: a free, open-source game engine.
Unity and Unreal Engine: the engines behind many games and XR apps; both are free to start learning.
Krita or GIMP: paint textures and images.
Audacity: record and edit sound.
VS Code: a free code editor.
Git and GitHub: save every version of your project and share it.
Hosting like Vercel, Netlify or itch.io: put your world online.

Blocks.Text: Pick one tool and finish one small project before adding the next.
Build the layout from plain boxes first, then walk through it. Studios call this a blockout or graybox.

Use real sizes. In this campus your eyes are 1.62 meters off the floor, doorways are 1.8 to 3.2 meters wide and ceilings are 3.4 to 7.6 meters high. You walk at 3 meters per second, about twice as fast as a real walk, because walking feels slow on a screen.
Move walls and rooms around until walking through feels good. Changing a box is quick; changing a finished building is not.
Every 3D model is a mesh: points in space (vertices) joined into triangles. A cube needs 12 triangles; a smooth sphere might use hundreds.

Artists usually model in Blender and export a file like glTF. This campus builds nearly everything from code instead: boxes, cylinders, spheres, lathed shapes like the lab flask and extruded shapes like roofs.
When a scene needs thousands of copies of one thing, like grass blades or books, instancing draws them all at once.
A material describes a surface. Physically based rendering (PBR) uses a few simple dials:

Items: Color (albedo): the surface’s own color.
Roughness: 0 is perfectly smooth and glossy (a mirror if it’s also metal), 1 is chalk.
Metalness: metal or not.
Normal map: fakes small bumps, like brick edges or wood grain, without extra triangles.

Blocks.Text: Textures are images wrapped onto meshes. Most textures here, from the bricks to the blueprints, are drawn by code onto a canvas as the campus loads.
Light makes a scene believable. Common kinds:

Items: Directional light: the sun. Parallel rays and crisp shadows.
Point lights: lamps that shine in every direction.
Image-based light: a picture of the sky or room that adds soft light and reflections.

Blocks.Text: Shadows are drawn from the light’s point of view into a shadow map. Lights cost speed: every lamp adds work to every lit pixel. This campus keeps 8 lamps switched on at once and moves them to the rooms near you.
Post effects run on the finished picture, like filters:

Items: Bloom: bright lights glow and bleed softly.
Ambient occlusion: darkens corners and creases where light can’t reach.
Tone mapping: squeezes very bright and very dark light into what a screen can show.
Color grading: sets the mood, like a filter on a photo.

Blocks.Text: Fog is different: it fades faraway things as each object is drawn, which hints at distance and hides the edge of the world.
Effects are seasoning. Set Graphics to Low in About to see the campus without bloom, ambient occlusion and grading.
A physics engine moves objects with gravity, mass, friction and collisions. Each object has a simple collider shape (a ball, a box or a capsule) that’s much cheaper to test than its full mesh.
The Recess Yard uses the Rapier physics engine and steps the world at a fixed 60 times per second, then smooths the motion between steps so it looks right at any frame rate.
To know what you tapped, the campus casts a ray, an invisible line, from the camera through your finger into the scene and finds the first thing it hits.
To walk you somewhere, it lays a grid over the floors and uses A* (A-star) pathfinding to find the shortest route around walls and furniture.
The virtual staff answer common questions from what the campus knows, and can use AI for harder ones when it’s allowed.
A smooth world draws a new frame about 60 times per second, which gives the computer about 16 milliseconds for each one.

Items: Fewer draw calls: merge objects that share a material, and use instancing for repeats.
Hide what you can’t see: this campus only draws rooms that are in view.
Quality levels: lower settings for older phones.
Dynamic resolution: draw fewer pixels when frames run slow, like many console games do.

Blocks.Text: Paste this into a file named index.html and open it in a browser. You’ll see a spinning box on grass.

<script type="importmap">{"imports":{"three":"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.170.0/build/three.module.js"}}</script>
<script type="module">
import * as THREE from 'three';
const scene = new THREE.Scene();
scene.background = new THREE.Color('#9cc3e4');
const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(60, innerWidth / innerHeight, 0.1, 100);
camera.position.set(0, 1.6, 5);
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true });
renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);
scene.add(new THREE.HemisphereLight('#ffffff', '#445533', 2));
const ground = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.PlaneGeometry(20, 20), new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: '#5d8f43' }));
ground.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2;
scene.add(ground);
const box = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1), new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: '#f2c14e' }));
box.position.y = 0.5;
scene.add(box);
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => { box.rotation.y += 0.01; renderer.render(scene, camera); });
</script>
Now change the color, add a second box, or move the camera. That’s world building.
Put your world online so people can try it, then watch them use it. Where do they get stuck? What do they love? Fix one thing at a time.
A learning path that works: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, then three.js, then Blender basics, then a weekend game jam with friends.
Jobs in this world include game developer, technical artist, 3D artist, level designer, XR developer and graphics engineer.

S01.Title: Welcome to the XRLibraries Campus
S01.Body: Three galleries and the Wax Hall tell XRLibraries’ story. After the museum, the tour visits the reading room, the four workshop rooms of the school and the Recess Yard. Margaret, the guide by the door, answers questions anytime.

S02.Title: Over 200 VR Systems in California Libraries
S02.Body: XRLibraries began in 2016 by installing more than 200 virtual reality systems in California public libraries. Its website calls this the largest VR installation in public libraries.

S03.Title: XR Made Easy for Everyone
S03.Body: XRLibraries works with schools and libraries to bring virtual, augmented and mixed reality into their programs and classes. Its stated goal is equitable access to immersive technology for all communities.

S04.Title: A Library VR Headset
S04.Body: Standalone headsets let a library visitor stand on the moon, swim a coral reef or practice a job, with no computer attached. Meta Quest and Pico both appear on XRLibraries’ partner list, and its Nevada headsets run on Pico.

S05.Title: Nevada Follows Marin County
S05.Body: In 2017 Nevada’s state library put its first VR headsets in public libraries: 22 headsets in 11 libraries, with STEM content. WorkingNation reports that the model followed a program at the Marin County Free Library in California.

S06.Title: XR at Computers in Libraries
S06.Body: XRLibraries’ executive director, John MacLeod, presented “Integrating XR Tech & Programming in Libraries” at Computers in Libraries Connect in 2020 and “Using XR to Discover ‘Lost Stories’ & Pop-Up Books” in 2022.

S07.Title: Project SANDI
S07.Body: Supporting and Advancing Nevada’s Dislocated Individuals began during the 2020 downturn with a $13.8 million federal grant. It uses VR to explore careers in five fields: skilled trades, healthcare, IT, advanced manufacturing and logistics.

S08.Title: 1,100 Headsets in Nevada
S08.Body: XRLibraries and Lifeliqe installed VR headsets in Nevada’s community college and public libraries. XRLibraries’ homepage counts more than 1,100.

S09.Title: Training From a Town of 300
S09.Body: A remote 12-week dialysis technician certification lets people train without traveling to a training center. In a community of about 300 people, a single mother finished the program, passed her certification and plans to become a registered nurse.

S10.Title: XR Playbooks
S10.Body: XRLibraries catalogs more than 300 XR apps in categories from astronomy and history to mindfulness and music, then bundles them into themed playbooks that come pre-installed on library headsets.

S11.Title: XR Showcase
S11.Body: In this video series, hosts George and Camila try VR and AR apps for libraries, from Tilt Brush and Wander to Apollo 11 VR, and share practical tips like cleaning headsets and setting a guardian boundary.

S12.Title: A Way Out of No Way
S12.Body: Marin City students who call themselves the Marinovators built a VR experience of the World War II shipyards and life in Marin City, plus a musical tribute to the African-American workers whose stories were rarely told.

S13.Title: The Black Wall Street of Charleston
S13.Body: Career and technical education students at Burke High School built an augmented-reality scavenger hunt that leads players to Charleston’s Black-owned businesses.

S14.Title: Seeking Immortality
S14.Body: A browser-based VR world, funded by an IMLS Native American Enhancement Grant, that preserves endangered Cheyenne language and cultural knowledge. Tribal members and students learned 3D scanning so the tribe keeps control of its own data.

S15.Title: Children Draw War, Not Flowers
S15.Body: An immersive 3D exhibition of art by children in Ukraine’s Cherkasy region, which took in more than 42,000 displaced children. It helps children work through war-related trauma, preserves their artwork, and was honored at the Anthem Awards.

S16.Title: Pollinators at the Marin County Fair
S16.Body: At XRLibraries’ bug-themed booth, fairgoers used an AR app called Pollinators to plant flowers and release monarch butterflies that flew around pollinating them. Marin artist Cynthia Jensen lent bug sculptures for the booth.

S17.Title: The Wax Hall
S17.Body: Through the doorway at the end of Gallery 3, wax figures act out XRLibraries’ story in twelve scenes, from the first VR stations in 2016 to the 2025 Marin County Fair. Each scene comes to life as you walk up. The figures are reenactors, not likenesses of real people.

S18.Title: The First Headsets
S18.Body: In 2016, libraries in Marin County, California, began offering virtual reality stations as the pilot for the California Virtual Reality Experience. XRLibraries launched that year as the project’s coordinator. Teen volunteers helped first-time visitors into headsets and guided them through their first worlds.

S19.Title: VR Goes Statewide
S19.Body: In June 2017 the California State Library, Oculus and the library consortium Califa partnered to bring VR-ready PCs with Rift headsets to more than 90 libraries across California, building on the Marin County pilot. XRLibraries, launched in 2016 as the project’s coordinator, also became a clearinghouse where libraries share what works with VR and AR.

S20.Title: Story Time in 3D
S20.Body: Library Journal reported in 2017 that young children loved virtual reality story times, while teens gravitated to VR games. In Marin, children listened to stories inside three-dimensional worlds.

S21.Title: Nevada Opens Its Stations
S21.Body: Nevada’s state library set aside $22,000 of a 2017 budget increase for a VR pilot: 22 headsets loaded with STEM content in 11 libraries, modeled on Marin County’s program. In February 2018 the Carson City Library’s grand re-opening featured VR and AR stations, and XRLibraries’ founder presented in a webinar for librarians across the state.

S22.Title: VR on the Road
S22.Body: Marin’s VR program went out into the community: to schools, senior centers, the county fair, and people displaced by deadly wildfires.

S23.Title: VR in the World’s Catalog
S23.Body: Nevada’s state library and its partner XRLibraries set out to catalog VR content so any library could find it. In 2019 Nevada librarians led a first-of-its-kind effort to catalog virtual reality in WorldCat, the world’s largest library catalog, and planned a cataloging hack-a-thon in Marin, California and Carson City, Nevada.

S24.Title: XR Marin and the XR Stars
S24.Body: XR Marin brought together the Marin County Free Library, XRLibraries, Novato Unified School District and the Marin County Office of Education. Teens served as “XR Stars,” helping patrons use the equipment. Its programs let people make 3D models, design 3D games and produce 360-degree video tours, and one teen at a VR summer camp borrowed the cameras and filmed her family’s farm.

S25.Title: Project SANDI
S25.Body: In October 2020 Nevada won a $13.8 million federal grant for Project SANDI (Supporting and Advancing Nevada’s Dislocated Individuals), which uses VR to explore careers in skilled trades, healthcare, IT, advanced manufacturing and logistics. It grew to more than 1,000 headsets at over 80 locations. XRLibraries’ executive director is a partner in the project.

S26.Title: 360° Stories in Washington
S26.Body: XRLibraries was the trainer for the Washington State Library’s VR 360 grant program. In 2022 it helped six libraries create 360-degree virtual reality stories about topics important to their communities. The program was open to public, tribal and academic libraries and funded by IMLS through the Library Services and Technology Act.

S27.Title: Lost Stories
S27.Body: In Marin City, students who call themselves the Marinovators built a VR experience of the World War II shipyards and life in Marin City, plus a musical tribute to the African-American workers whose stories were rarely told. XRLibraries’ director presented its Lost Stories work at Computers in Libraries in 2022.

S28.Title: Children Draw War, Not Flowers
S28.Body: XRLibraries helped design “Children Draw War, Not Flowers,” a browser-based VR art exhibition from the San José State University School of Information. It shows art by Ukrainian children aged 4 to 16 and virtual galleries showing the destruction of Ukrainian libraries, and anyone can visit it free in a web browser.

S29.Title: Pollinators at the Fair
S29.Body: At the 2025 Marin County Fair, XRLibraries’ bug-themed booth featured Pollinators, an augmented-reality app where fairgoers planted flowers and released monarch butterflies that flew around pollinating them. Marin artist Cynthia Jensen lent bug sculptures for the booth.

S30.Title: The Reading Room
S30.Body: The library has 15 short books about XR and more, open to read on the featured table and on the ends of the stacks. Rosa at the reference desk answers questions from them.

S31.Title: Room 101: 3D Art Studio
S31.Body: Every class in the Workshop School is a hands-on workshop. Here you paint in the air with neon, chrome, ribbon and rainbow brushes, stamp 3D shapes, mirror your strokes and switch to a blank canvas.

S32.Title: Room 102: Science Lab
S32.Body: A working lab with goggles on. Run a sieve analysis to measure the grain sizes in a sand sample, find the concentration of a mystery acid by titration, and measure gravity with a pendulum.

S33.Title: Room 103: Blueprint Lab
S33.Body: Five real-world blueprints: a car, an excavator, a house, a truss bridge and a computer. Tap any part to learn its name, what it does and how you could build a model, then build a model car or building at the bench.

S34.Title: Room 104: World Builder Studio
S34.Body: How do you build a world like this campus? Build a mini world on the layer table one step at a time, from a sketch to a live website, and read the World Builder’s Handbook to start your own.

S35.Title: The Recess Yard
S35.DateLabel: Out the back of the school
S35.Body: Recess is for fun in XR: ride the Comet Coaster, take the Sky Drop for a view of the whole campus, or go on an Ocean Dive with sea creatures. Coach Rae can help, and XR tokens are hidden all over the campus.

what.Body: XRLibraries brings virtual, augmented and mixed reality into libraries and schools. Its stated goal is equitable access to immersive technology for all communities. It began in 2016 and is based in Novato, in Marin County, California.

who.Body: John MacLeod is the executive director of XRLibraries. He works with state and local libraries on plans for virtual reality, augmented reality and 360 video, and he is building a national clearinghouse where libraries can share XR best practices.

team.Body: The XRLibraries About page lists John MacLeod as executive director, Dane Lancaster of PacificXR, who led the setup of XRMarin as an immersive learning lab, and George Lightfoot and Camila Oates, the XR Showcase team.

wsl.Body: XRLibraries was the trainer for the Washington State Library’s VR 360 grant program, which in 2022 helped six libraries create 360-degree virtual reality stories about topics important to their communities. The program was funded by IMLS through the Library Services and Technology Act and was open to public, tribal and academic libraries.

freedom.Body: Freedom to Read is a VR environment built with the SJSU School of Information, Unite Against Book Bans, Little Free Library and Books Unbanned. It helps people fight book bans and helps young people find challenged books that reflect their lives.

environment.Body: XRLibraries’ environment projects include the Stanford Ocean Experience, a VR experience about ocean acidification; a Climate Change Playbook of VR apps for viewing and discussion; and Hydrous, which takes visitors to the coral reefs of Palau.

partners.Body: Partners listed on xrlibraries.com include Meta Quest, Pico, Hydrous, the Washington, Nevada and California state libraries, ALA, Internet Librarian, the Marin County Office of Education, XRMarin, New Media Learning, FastForward and the SJSU School of Information.

sjsu.Body: XRLibraries is a strategic partner of the Library Technology Integration Lab at the San José State University School of Information.

xrmarin.Body: XRMarin is an immersive learning lab and academy for creating XR content in Marin County. XRLibraries’ director is a partner in the Marinovation Learning Center and the XRMarin academy.

concept.Body: This campus is an unofficial concept made by Ev Holt with Walk the Archive for XRLibraries. Its facts come from public sources such as xrlibraries.com, the SJSU School of Information, WorkingNation and ArborXR.

yard.Body: The campus’s Recess Yard has three made-up rides for fun in XR: the Comet Coaster roller coaster, the Sky Drop tower and the Ocean Dive, a guided swim with sea creatures. Visitors can also hunt for hidden XR tokens and unlock badges.

school.Body: The campus’s Workshop School has four hands-on rooms. Room 101 is the 3D Art Studio, where you paint and stamp shapes in the air. Room 102 is the Science Lab, with a sieve analysis of sand, an acid–base titration and a pendulum. Room 103 is the Blueprint Lab, with blueprints of a car, an excavator, a house, a truss bridge and a computer, and a bench for building models. Room 104 is the World Builder Studio, which shows how a 3D world like this campus gets made.

wax.Body: The museum’s Wax Hall, through the doorway at the end of Gallery 3, is a living-history wing. Twelve scenes of wax figures act out XRLibraries’ story in date order, from the first VR stations in Marin County’s libraries in 2016 to the Pollinators booth at the 2025 Marin County Fair. Each scene comes to life when you walk up to it. The figures are reenactors made for this concept, not likenesses of real people.

history.Body: XRLibraries began in 2016 as the coordinator of the California Virtual Reality Experience, which piloted VR stations in Marin County’s libraries. In 2017 the project spread to more than 90 California libraries, and a pilot in Nevada followed. Later milestones include Nevada’s first VR records in WorldCat in 2019, Project SANDI in 2020, 360-degree storytelling training in Washington in 2022 and the Pollinators AR booth at the 2025 Marin County Fair.

wta.Body: Walk the Archive is Ev Holt’s tool for turning a library’s, museum’s or tribe’s collection into a place you can walk through in a web browser, on a phone, a laptop or a library computer.

lesson-1.Title: How a sieve test works: sieve analysis, particle size distribution, PSD
lesson-1.Body: A sieve analysis measures particle size distribution, or PSD: how much of a sample falls in each size range. You split out a representative sample, dry it and weigh it, then shake it through a stack of sieves, coarsest on top and finest at the bottom, and weigh what each sieve holds. Sand and gravel producers use sieve tests to check that their product meets its size specification.

lesson-2.Title: Sieve mesh numbers and openings
lesson-2.Body: A sieve’s mesh number counts the openings per inch, so a bigger number means a finer sieve. A US number 20 sieve has 850 micrometer openings, a number 40 has 425 and a number 100 has 150. One micrometer is a thousandth of a millimeter.

lesson-3.Title: Cumulative percent passing and D50
lesson-3.Body: For each sieve you work out the percent retained, add them up from the top to get the cumulative percent retained, and subtract from 100 to get the percent passing. D50 is the grain size that half the sample is finer than. D10 and D60 give the uniformity coefficient, Cu = D60 ÷ D10; a Cu near 1 means the grains are nearly all the same size.

lesson-4.Title: AFS grain fineness number GFN
lesson-4.Body: The AFS grain fineness number, or GFN, multiplies the percent retained on each sieve by a factor for that sieve, adds them up and divides by the total percent retained. A higher number means finer sand. Foundries use it to describe molding sand.

lesson-5.Title: Checking a finished sieve run for lost mass
lesson-5.Body: After a sieve test, the sieve weights should add back up to the starting weight. ASTM C136, a standard sieve test for aggregates, says that if the difference is more than 0.3 percent of the starting dry mass, the results should not be used for acceptance testing.

lesson-6.Title: Acid base titration
lesson-6.Body: In a titration you add a solution of known concentration from a burette, a little at a time, until it exactly reacts with your sample. An indicator such as phenolphthalein turns pink when the solution turns basic, which marks the endpoint. For an acid like HCl reacting with NaOH, moles of base equal moles of acid, so the acid’s molarity = base molarity × base volume ÷ acid volume.

lesson-7.Title: pH and the equivalence point
lesson-7.Body: pH measures how acidic a solution is: 7 is neutral, lower is acidic and higher is basic, and each step of 1 is a tenfold change. When a strong acid is titrated with a strong base, the pH jumps sharply near the equivalence point, where the moles of base added equal the moles of acid.

lesson-8.Title: Pendulum period and gravity
lesson-8.Body: A simple pendulum’s period, the time for one full swing out and back, is about T = 2π√(L/g) for small swings. It depends on the length, not the mass. Time 10 swings and divide by 10 for a better measurement. Plot T² against L for a few lengths, and the slope equals 4π²/g, so g = 4π² ÷ slope, about 9.8 meters per second squared on Earth.

lesson-9.Title: Rubber band car model
lesson-9.Body: A rubber-band car stores energy in a stretched rubber band. As the band unwinds, it turns the rear axle and drives the car forward. Drinking straws make good bearings, so the axles spin with little friction. Test it, change one thing at a time and test again.

lesson-10.Title: Cross bracing and shake tables
lesson-10.Body: Cross-bracing turns a frame’s rectangles into triangles, and a triangle can’t change shape unless a side changes length, so a braced frame resists racking in earthquakes and wind. Engineers test buildings and models on shake tables that move back and forth like an earthquake.

lesson-11.Title: How to build a 3D world
lesson-11.Body: A 3D world gets built in layers: plan it, block it out with plain boxes, model the shapes, add materials, light it, add effects like glow and fog, add physics, add life like people and rides, then publish it and improve it. This campus runs in a web browser using three.js for 3D and the Rapier physics engine for the playground.

sieve.Title: Sieve analysis (PSD)
sieve.Subtitle: Measure the grain sizes in sand
StepTexts: A sieve analysis measures how big the grains in a sample are. Labs report it as the particle size distribution, or PSD. Sand plants, concrete labs and foundries rely on this test to check their materials.

A pile of sand isn’t the same all the way through: big grains and fine grains separate. Pour it through the riffle splitter, which divides it into two matching halves, keep one half, and split again until you have about 100 grams.

Dry the sample in the oven at about 110 °C until its mass stops changing, and let it cool. Then press TARE with the empty dish on the balance, so the reading only counts the sand, and pour the sample in.

Nest the sieves with the biggest openings on top and the finest at the bottom, with a pan underneath to catch the dust. Sieves are named by their US mesh number, roughly the number of openings per inch.

Pour the sample onto the top sieve, put the cover on, clamp the stack and press START. The shaker swirls and taps the stack so every grain gets its chance to fall through. Labs often shake for 10 to 15 minutes; this run is sped up.
Lift the sieves off one at a time, from the top, and weigh what stayed on each. The balance is tared for each empty sieve, so it reads the retained mass.

The AFS grain fineness number sums each sieve’s % retained times a multiplier, then divides by the total. A bigger number means finer sand. Plants compare it, and the whole curve, against each customer’s spec.

titration.Title: Acid–base titration
titration.Subtitle: Find the concentration of a mystery acid
StepTexts: A titration finds how concentrated a solution is by reacting it with another solution whose concentration you already know. Here, sodium hydroxide (a base) neutralizes a mystery hydrochloric acid.
Phenolphthalein, the indicator, stays colorless in acid and turns pink once the solution turns slightly basic, at about pH 8.2.

Pour exactly 25.00 mL of the mystery acid into the flask and add 2 drops of phenolphthalein. Fill the burette with 0.1000 M sodium hydroxide, then read the starting volume at the bottom of the curved liquid surface, the meniscus, with your eye level with it.

Hold the flask and swirl it as the base runs in. Add base fast at first. When pink flashes start to linger, slow down and finish one drop at a time. The endpoint is the first drop that keeps the whole flask faint pink for 30 seconds.

pendulum.Title: Pendulum
pendulum.Subtitle: Measure gravity with a string and a weight
Steps: Set the length and let go
StepTexts: A pendulum’s swing time depends on its length and on gravity, but not on how heavy the bob is. Time 10 full swings, and you can work out the strength of gravity, g.
The math: one swing takes T = 2π√(L ÷ g), so g = 4π²L ÷ T².
Set the length from the pivot to the center of the bob. Then take hold of the bob, pull it back to the release angle, keep it still and let go. The photogate counts 10 full swings (there and back).
Swinging… The photogate times each pass. Let it finish 10 full swings.

bench.Title: Model bench
bench.Subtitle: Build a model car or building
StepTexts: Stiff cardboard or foam board, 2 drinking straws, 2 wooden skewers, 4 bottle caps, a rubber band, a paper clip, tape and glue. It’s all in the kit box. Good engineers start with a plan and a parts list.

Take the cardboard rectangle, about 20 by 8 centimeters, and rest it on the little stand so you can work underneath. This is the chassis, the frame everything else attaches to. A stiff, light chassis wastes less energy bending.
Tape the two straws across the bottom, one near each end. Keep them parallel or the car will curve. The straws are bearings: the axles spin inside them with very little friction.
Slide a skewer through each straw, leaving a little sticking out on both sides. Axles carry the wheels and let each pair turn together.
Poke a hole in the center of each bottle cap and push one onto each axle end. A dab of glue keeps them on. Wheels that are centered and straight roll farther and wobble less.

Hook the rubber band on a paper clip taped to the front, and loop the other end around the rear axle. The stretched rubber band stores energy. As it unwinds it spins the rear axle: your engine and drivetrain in one.
Fold a body from card stock and set it over the chassis. Keep it light. Less weight lets the same stored energy push the car farther.
Roll the car backward to wind the band around the axle, set it down and let go! Real engineers test, measure, change one thing and test again.
Panel: Pick a kit. You’ll build it with your own hands, one part at a time, the way you would with real materials, then test it.

diorama.Title: Layer table
diorama.Subtitle: Build a mini world, one layer at a time
StepTexts: Every world starts as an idea and a sketch. Who is it for, and what will they do there? This campus started as a list (a museum, a library, a school and a recess yard) and a rough map of how to walk between them.
Build the layout from plain boxes, then walk around it. Is the hall wide enough? Does the coaster fit? Fixing things now is cheap. Game studios call this a blockout, or graybox.

Swap the boxes for real models. Artists build them in tools like Blender; this campus builds almost everything from code: boxes, cylinders, spheres and extruded shapes. Every model is a mesh of triangles. Turn on X-ray to see them.

Materials say what a surface is made of: its color, how rough or shiny it is, and whether it’s metal. Physically based materials (PBR) react to light the way real surfaces do. Many of the textures here are drawn by code as the campus loads.

Light sells the scene. Outdoors, a sun casts shadows and the sky tints everything; indoors, lamps take over. Lights are expensive to draw, so this campus keeps just 8 lamps switched on and moves them to wherever you are.
Post effects are the finishing pass over the whole picture: glow (bloom) around bright lights, soft shading in corners (ambient occlusion) and color grading.
A physics engine moves things with gravity, mass and collisions. The Recess Yard runs a physics engine called Rapier, stepping the world 60 times a second. Drop some balls and watch them bounce.
Life makes a world feel real: people who move, rides that run and things you can tap. Tapping works by casting a ray from your finger into the scene; walking uses A* (A-star) pathfinding on a grid.
Ship it! This whole campus is one web page, with no app store and no download, so it runs on phones, Chromebooks and laptops. Then watch real people use it, listen, and make it better.

dx-hygiene.Title: Hand hygiene and PPE
dx-hygiene.Subtitle: Where every treatment begins and ends
StepTexts: A dialysis patient's bloodstream is opened at every treatment, so the single most effective protection against infection is clean hands. Every session begins and ends at this sink.
Wet your hands, soap them, and scrub for at least twenty seconds: palms, backs, between the fingers and under the nails. Rinse, dry with a paper towel, and use the towel to turn off the tap.
Gloves go on last and come off first. A gown and a face shield protect you wherever a line could spray. Change gloves between every patient and every task.
A technician keeps a clean field, the supplies and the machine's connections, and a dirty one, the used lines and the bins. Nothing crosses back from dirty to clean.

Wet your hands, soap them, and scrub for at least twenty seconds: palms, backs, between the fingers and under the nails. Rinse, dry with a paper towel, and use the towel to turn off the tap.
Gloves go on last and come off first. A gown and a face shield protect you wherever a line could spray. Change gloves between every patient and every task.

dx-machine.Title: The dialysis machine
dx-machine.Subtitle: Prime it, fit the dialyzer, check the prescription
StepTexts: A pump moves the patient's blood through the dialyzer, where waste and extra water pass into the dialysate, and the cleaned blood returns. The machine watches pressures, temperature and conductivity the whole time.
Turn the machine on and let it run its own checks: the alarms, the pumps, the air detector. A machine that fails a check is not used that day.
Hang the saline, thread the blood lines through the pump and the air detector, and prime them until no bubbles remain. Air in the line is the alarm you never want to hear.
The cartridge is the artificial kidney: thousands of hollow fibres in a clear case. Fit it in its holder, connect the lines and check that it is the type the order asks for.
The patient's dialysate mix, flow rate, treatment time and fluid removal are set from the order. Every number is read twice, and the second reading is by a second person.

The carbon tanks take out chlorine and chloramine, the softener takes out hardness, and reverse osmosis takes out nearly everything else. Each stage protects the next.

easel.Title: 3D Art Studio
easel.Subtitle: Paint in the air with brushes, shapes and symmetry
StepTexts: Seven brushes hang on the easel: neon, paint, ribbon, chrome, rainbow, beads and sparkle. Each leaves a different trail in the air. Start with paint.
Hold the trigger and move your hand: the stroke hangs where you drew it. Step round it. A stroke in the air has a front, a back and sides, like a sculpture.
Stamp a cube, a sphere, a cone, a ring, a star or a heart, and switch on symmetry to mirror every stroke across the easel.
Spin the turntable to see your piece from every side, then save a picture of it. Walk-around art is what XR studios make.
